vpop_roster has one row per virtual patient, 4 PK ETAs, 51 QSP ETAs, and the PK covariates. The PK draw preserves the loaded model’s full OMEGA, including its Vc/ke covariance. Within QSP, the three Th2 ETAs are drawn jointly and 48 remain independent. No cross-model PK-QSP correlation is imposed. Merging these ETAs and covariates into later event tables holds patient identity fixed across dosing scenarios; covariates are not ETA columns.

cat("cor(etacl, etalk1)   [PK vs. unrelated QSP eta, expect ~0]:  ", cor(vpop_roster$eta.ke, vpop_roster$etalk1), "\n")
## cor(etacl, etalk1)   [PK vs. unrelated QSP eta, expect ~0]:   0.006791965
cat("cor(etalk11, etalk13) [Th2 block, expect ~", rho, "]:          ", cor(vpop_roster$etalk11, vpop_roster$etalk13), "\n")
## cor(etalk11, etalk13) [Th2 block, expect ~ 0.6 ]:           0.5976676
cat("cor(etalk11, etalk19) [Th2 block, expect ~", rho, "]:          ", cor(vpop_roster$etalk11, vpop_roster$etalk19), "\n")
## cor(etalk11, etalk19) [Th2 block, expect ~ 0.6 ]:           0.6155764
df_check <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = vpop_roster$eta.ke, y = vpop_roster$etalk1,
             panel = "PK etacl vs. QSP etalk1 (independent)"),
  data.frame(x = vpop_roster$etalk11, y = vpop_roster$etalk13,
             panel = "QSP etalk11 vs. etalk13 (correlated Th2 block)")
)
ggplot(df_check, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "vpop_roster structure check: independent by default, correlated where explicitly built")

This vpop_roster is the joint sampling infrastructure used in the dose-response exercise below.

6 Integrated dose-response analysis

Miyano 2022, as published, has no dose axis at all – each drug arm is a fixed inhibition fraction, not a function of mg administered. This section builds a genuine dose-response curve three ways, using the vpop_roster joint sampling from above so that each virtual patient’s identity (both PK and QSP parameters) is held fixed across every dose level.

6.1 (a) Fixed-inhibition response (no dose axis)

As a baseline, the closest thing to a “dose-response” the published model supports is sweeping the inhibition fraction itself as a synthetic dose proxy (there being no real dose to sweep):

inhibition_levels <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99)

dose_response_a <- purrr::map_dfr(inhibition_levels, function(r_val) {
  ev <- rxode2::et(seq(0, 24, by = 1)) |> rxode2::et(id = seq_len(n_per_arm))
  ev$cmt <- "barrier"
  p <- c(r_placebo = 1, r_il4 = r_val, r_il13 = r_val, r_il17 = 0, r_il22 = 0,
         r_il31 = 0, r_tslp = 0, r_ox40l = 0, c_rifng = 0, e_a2 = 1)
  sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_stoch, events = ev, nSub = n_per_arm, params = p,
                         inits = baseline_typ_named) |> as.data.frame()
  sim$inhibition <- r_val
  sim
})

baseline_a <- dose_response_a |> dplyr::filter(time == 0) |>
  dplyr::select(inhibition, id, EASI_baseline = EASI)
dose_response_a <- dose_response_a |>
  dplyr::left_join(baseline_a, by = c("inhibition", "id")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct_improved = 100 * (EASI_baseline - EASI) / EASI_baseline)

easi75_a <- dose_response_a |>
  dplyr::filter(time == 24) |>
  dplyr::group_by(inhibition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(EASI75 = 100 * mean(pct_improved > 75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(easi75_a, aes(x = inhibition, y = EASI75)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Fixed cytokine-inhibition fraction (r_il4 = r_il13; a synthetic \"dose\" proxy)",
       y = "Week-24 EASI-75 responder rate (%)",
       title = "(a) Miyano-style rudimentary dose-response",
       caption = paste0("n = ", n_per_arm, " per level; no real dose or PK axis exists in the published model."))

This curve answers a different question than a true dose-response: it shows how EASI-75 depends on an assumed inhibition fraction, not on how much drug (mg) was administered or how that translates to target engagement over time.

6.2 (b) PK-linked dose-response

Using vpop_roster, the same 1000 virtual patients are dosed at five exploratory maintenance-dose levels. Each loading dose is twice its maintenance dose, so the 300 mg arm uses the labeled 600 mg load plus 300 mg q2w regimen. PK time is in days and QSP time is in weeks: seven days per week converts the q2w interval to 14 days, and PK observation times are converted back to weeks before joining QSP events. The Emax link is illustrative.

Each point on this curve is a responder-rate estimate from one finite virtual cohort (n_roster = 1000 patients), so it carries sampling uncertainty just like an observed rate from a real trial would. Because the per-patient outcomes are already fully simulated below, a nonparametric (case-resampling) bootstrap is the cheapest way to quantify that uncertainty: resample the n_roster patients’ already-simulated pct_improved outcomes with replacement, recompute the EASI-75 proportion, repeat many times, and take the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles of the resulting distribution. This needs no new ODE solves – only resampling numbers already in hand – unlike a parametric bootstrap that would redraw fresh ETAs and re-run rxSolve() for every replicate.

dose_levels <- c(100, 200, 300, 450, 600)  # maintenance SC dose (mg), q2w; loading = 2x maintenance (same structure as the labeled regimen above)
days_per_week <- 7
maintenance_interval_days <- 2 * days_per_week
pk_observation_days <- t_grid * days_per_week
simulate_dose <- function(maintenance_dose) {
  # PK: same cohort size. etaka/etacl/etav covariates from vpop_roster (see technique note above).
  ev_pk_dose <- rxode2::et(amt = 2 * maintenance_dose, time = 0, cmt = "depot", id = seq_len(n_roster)) |>
    rxode2::et(amt = maintenance_dose, time = maintenance_interval_days,
          ii = maintenance_interval_days, addl = 11, cmt = "depot") |>
    rxode2::et(pk_observation_days)
  ev_pk_dose <- as.data.frame(ev_pk_dose) |>
    dplyr::left_join(vpop_roster |> dplyr::select(id, all_of(pk_eta_names),WT:WHITE), by = "id")
  pk_dose_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(pk_dupi, events = ev_pk_dose) |>
    mutate(conc=cp) |>
    as.data.frame()

  pk_dose_cov <- pk_dose_sim |>
    dplyr::transmute(id, time = time / days_per_week,
                     r_il4  = Emax * conc / (EC50 + conc),
                     r_il13 = Emax * conc / (EC50 + conc))

  # QSP: same t_grid/cohort, QSP ETAs pinned per patient via vpop_roster,
  # PK-derived time-varying r_il4/r_il13 covariate merged in alongside them.
  ev_qsp_dose <- rxode2::et(t_grid) |> rxode2::et(id = seq_len(n_roster))
  ev_qsp_dose$cmt <- "barrier"
  ev_qsp_dose <- as.data.frame(ev_qsp_dose) |>
    dplyr::left_join(pk_dose_cov, by = c("id", "time")) |>
    dplyr::left_join(vpop_roster |> dplyr::select(id, dplyr::all_of(names(qsp_omega_diag))), by = "id")

  p_dose_other <- c(r_placebo = 1, r_il17 = 0, r_il22 = 0, r_il31 = 0,
                    r_tslp = 0, r_ox40l = 0, c_rifng = 0, e_a2 = 1)

  qsp_dose_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_stoch, events = ev_qsp_dose,
                                  params = p_dose_other,
                                  inits = baseline_typ_named) |> as.data.frame()
  qsp_dose_sim$dose <- maintenance_dose
  qsp_dose_sim
}

dose_response_b <- purrr::map_dfr(dose_levels, simulate_dose)

baseline_b <- dose_response_b |> dplyr::filter(time == 0) |>
  dplyr::select(dose, id, EASI_baseline = EASI)
dose_response_b <- dose_response_b |>
  dplyr::left_join(baseline_b, by = c("dose", "id")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct_improved = 100 * (EASI_baseline - EASI) / EASI_baseline)

# Nonparametric (case-resampling) bootstrap 95% CI on the week-24 EASI-75
# responder rate at each dose: resample the n_roster patients' already-
# simulated pct_improved outcomes with replacement, recompute the responder
# proportion, repeat n_boot times, and take percentiles. This captures
# sampling uncertainty from having a finite virtual cohort; it does NOT
# capture parameter uncertainty in the model's own THETA/OMEGA estimates
# (see the interpretation note below).
set.seed(9090)
n_boot <- 500L

boot_easi75 <- function(pct_improved, n_boot) {
  n <- length(pct_improved)
  point_est <- 100 * mean(pct_improved > 75, na.rm = TRUE)
  boot_props <- replicate(n_boot, {
    100 * mean(sample(pct_improved, n, replace = TRUE) > 75, na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  tibble::tibble(EASI75 = point_est,
                lower = unname(quantile(boot_props, 0.025)),
                upper = unname(quantile(boot_props, 0.975)))
}

easi75_b <- dose_response_b |>
  dplyr::filter(time == 24) |>
  dplyr::group_by(dose) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(~ boot_easi75(.x$pct_improved, n_boot)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

ggplot(easi75_b, aes(x = dose, y = EASI75)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.15, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 3) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Maintenance dose (mg SC, q2w; loading = 2x)",
       y = "Week-24 EASI-75 responder rate (%)",
      title = "(b) Integrated PopPK + PopSP dose-response, with bootstrap 95% CI",
       caption = paste0("Point = observed responder rate across n = ", n_roster,
                        " virtual patients (vpop_roster, reused across every dose level); ",
                        "ribbon = nonparametric bootstrap 95% CI (", n_boot, " resamples)."))

Unlike (a), this curve has an administered mg dose axis. Each point reflects the same virtual patients’ PK and QSP draws propagated through concentration and the illustrative Emax link. Use the rendered values to assess the shape; a plateau or separation between dose levels is a model prediction, not evidence of clinical dose equivalence.

Interpreting the ribbon: the bootstrap band only reflects finite-cohort sampling uncertainty in the responder-rate estimate – it answers “how much would this curve wiggle if I re-drew a different random sample of n_roster patients from the same simulated distribution?” It does not propagate uncertainty in the underlying model itself (e.g. the paper’s fitted THETA/OMEGA values, or the illustrative PK submodel’s parameters). Quantifying that structural/parameter uncertainty would require a parametric bootstrap or a full uncertainty analysis on the original model fits, which is out of scope for this tutorial.

6.3 Exercise 5: Integrated mechanisms and illustrative dose selection

Better together: regimen -> exposure -> inhibition -> disease response. PopPK predicts patient-specific exposure; the illustrative exposure-effect link translates it into inhibition; QSP predicts EASI-75 response. PopPK alone cannot predict EASI-75, and fixed-inhibition QSP alone cannot connect that response to an administered mg dose. Integration enables this dose-selection exercise, but does not automatically validate a clinical recommendation.

6.3.1 Part A: Fixed vs. PK-driven inhibition

dose_response_b already contains the PK-driven mechanism’s result at the labeled 300 mg maintenance dose (the dose == 300 rows). Build the matching fixed-inhibition comparator – the same vpop_roster virtual patients (same PopSP ETAs), same t_grid, but with r_il4 = r_il13 = 0.99 held constant for the whole 24 weeks instead of the PK-driven time-varying value – and compare the two EASI-75 curves. Because both mechanisms now reuse the same vpop_roster PopSP ETAs, any difference you see is attributable only to the drug-effect mechanism, not to different patients.

Compare the onset and week-24 response. Why can a PK-driven mechanism respond to changes in administered dose or interval, whereas a fixed 0.99 inhibition assumption cannot? Use this distinction to explain why the models are better together for Part B’s mg-based efficacy question.

# Suggested answer: fixed-inhibition comparator using the SAME vpop_roster
# PopSP ETAs as dose_response_b (dose == 300), so the two mechanisms are
# compared on identical virtual patients.
ev_fixed_matched <- rxode2::et(t_grid) |> rxode2::et(id = seq_len(n_roster))
ev_fixed_matched$cmt <- "barrier"
ev_fixed_matched <- as.data.frame(ev_fixed_matched) |>
  dplyr::left_join(vpop_roster |> dplyr::select(id, dplyr::all_of(names(qsp_omega_diag))), by = "id")
p_fixed_matched <- c(r_placebo = 1, r_il4 = 0.99, r_il13 = 0.99, r_il17 = 0, r_il22 = 0,
                     r_il31 = 0, r_tslp = 0, r_ox40l = 0, c_rifng = 0, e_a2 = 1)
fixed_matched_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_stoch, events = ev_fixed_matched,
                                     params = p_fixed_matched,
                                     inits = baseline_typ_named) |> as.data.frame()

easi75_from_matched <- function(sim, label) {
  baseline_easi <- sim |> dplyr::filter(time == 0) |> dplyr::select(id, EASI_baseline0 = EASI)
  sim |>
    dplyr::select(-dplyr::any_of("EASI_baseline"), -dplyr::any_of("pct_improved")) |>
    dplyr::left_join(baseline_easi, by = "id") |>
    dplyr::mutate(pct_improved = 100 * (EASI_baseline0 - EASI) / EASI_baseline0) |>
    dplyr::group_by(time) |>
    dplyr::summarise(EASI75 = 100 * mean(pct_improved > 75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(mechanism = label)
}

easi75_matched_compare <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dose_response_b |> dplyr::filter(dose == 300) |>
    easi75_from_matched("PK-driven (300 mg q2w)"),
  easi75_from_matched(fixed_matched_sim, "Fixed inhibition (r_il4 = r_il13 = 0.99)")
)

p <- ggplot(easi75_matched_compare, aes(x = time, y = EASI75, colour = mechanism)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position="bottom")+
  labs(x = "Time on treatment (weeks)", y = "EASI-75 responder rate (%)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Fixed inhibition vs. PK-driven inhibition, same virtual patients, matched 300 mg dose",
       caption = "Both mechanisms reuse vpop_roster's PopSP ETAs -- only the drug-effect mechanism differs.")
p

get_val_m <- function(df, wk, mech) round(df$EASI75[df$time == wk & df$mechanism == mech], 0)
cat("Week 2  -- PK-driven:", get_val_m(easi75_matched_compare, 2, "PK-driven (300 mg q2w)"),
    "%  Fixed:", get_val_m(easi75_matched_compare, 2, "Fixed inhibition (r_il4 = r_il13 = 0.99)"), "%\n")
## Week 2  -- PK-driven: 43 %  Fixed: 58 %
cat("Week 24 -- PK-driven:", get_val_m(easi75_matched_compare, 24, "PK-driven (300 mg q2w)"),
    "%  Fixed:", get_val_m(easi75_matched_compare, 24, "Fixed inhibition (r_il4 = r_il13 = 0.99)"), "%\n")
## Week 24 -- PK-driven: 57 %  Fixed: 64 %

The PK-driven mechanism lags behind the fixed-inhibition mechanism early in treatment (the inhibition fraction is still ramping up through the SC absorption phase, while the fixed mechanism is unrealistically already at full 0.99 blockade from t = 0), and does not fully converge to the fixed mechanism’s ceiling by week 24 (the accumulated multi-dose concentration plateaus a little below full saturation of the Emax relationship). The qualitative lesson generalizes beyond dupilumab: treating drug effect as an instantaneous constant systematically overstates early-treatment response relative to a model that links a real absorption/distribution/elimination profile to target engagement.

6.3.2 Part B: An illustrative RP2D recommendation

First, read easi75_b and the plot: identify the largest estimated week-24 responder rate, compare the 300 mg arm with its neighboring doses, and explain what the bootstrap band includes and excludes. Does overlap establish clinical equivalence?

Why the lowest tested dose near the best response? If increasing dose buys little additional predicted efficacy, the extra drug may not be worthwhile. This is an efficacy-efficiency trade-off, not proof that a lower dose is safer. We select among tested doses because intermediate doses have not been simulated; the loading dose remains twice maintenance.

For this classroom exercise, select the lowest tested maintenance dose whose predicted week-24 EASI-75 rate is within 5 percentage points of the highest predicted rate. The 5-point margin is a teaching assumption, not a clinically justified threshold. Apply it to point estimates, not to overlapping confidence bands.

  1. Using easi75_b, make a table of maintenance dose, EASI-75 rate, difference from the best rate, and eligibility. Report the selected dose q2w and its twice-maintenance loading dose.
  2. Repeat with margins of 0 and 10 percentage points. Does the choice change? No new simulations are needed.
  3. Read the supplied recommendation below. Explain why it is an illustrative recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D) candidate, not a clinical recommendation; no written recommendation is required.

The margins (0, 5, and 10 percentage points) are classroom sensitivity settings; the loading multiplier of 2 comes from the regimen definition in simulate_dose().

rp2d_margin_pp <- 5
rp2d_sensitivity_margins_pp <- c(0, rp2d_margin_pp, 10)
rp2d_loading_multiplier <- 2

rp2d_table <- function(response, margin_pp) {
  stopifnot(nrow(response) > 0,
            all(is.finite(response$dose)), all(response$dose > 0),
            !anyDuplicated(response$dose),
            all(is.finite(response$EASI75)),
            all(response$EASI75 >= 0 & response$EASI75 <= 100),
            length(margin_pp) == 1, is.finite(margin_pp), margin_pp >= 0)
  decision <- response |>
    dplyr::select(dose, EASI75) |>
    dplyr::arrange(dose) |>
    dplyr::mutate(gap_pp = max(EASI75) - EASI75,
                  eligible = gap_pp <= margin_pp)
  decision |>
    dplyr::mutate(selected = dose == min(dose[eligible]))
}

rp2d_decision <- rp2d_table(easi75_b, rp2d_margin_pp)
knitr::kable(rp2d_decision, digits = 1,
             col.names = c('Maintenance (mg q2w)', 'EASI-75 (%)',
                           'Gap from best (pp)', 'Eligible', 'Selected'))
Maintenance (mg q2w) EASI-75 (%) Gap from best (pp) Eligible Selected
100 39.3 20.6 FALSE FALSE
200 52.9 7.0 FALSE FALSE
300 56.6 3.3 TRUE TRUE
450 58.9 1.0 TRUE FALSE
600 59.9 0.0 TRUE FALSE 
rp2d_sensitivity <- purrr::map_dfr(rp2d_sensitivity_margins_pp, function(margin_pp) {
  rp2d_table(easi75_b, margin_pp) |>
    dplyr::filter(selected) |>
    dplyr::transmute(margin_pp, maintenance_mg = dose,
                     loading_mg = rp2d_loading_multiplier * dose, EASI75)
})
knitr::kable(rp2d_sensitivity, digits = 1,
             col.names = c('Margin (pp)', 'Maintenance (mg q2w)',
                           'Loading (mg)', 'EASI-75 (%)'))
Margin (pp) Maintenance (mg q2w) Loading (mg) EASI-75 (%)
0 600 1200 59.9
5 300 600 56.6
10 200 400 52.9 
rp2d_candidate <- rp2d_sensitivity |>
  dplyr::filter(margin_pp == rp2d_margin_pp)

Illustrative RP2D recommendation. Under the classroom rule, our candidate is 300 mg SC q2w after a 600 mg loading dose. This is an efficacy-only model exercise, not a clinical RP2D recommendation: safety and tolerability are not assessed, and the exposure-effect link is illustrative.

The rule selects a candidate only within this tested grid and this virtual cohort. Increasing the margin can retain or lower the selected dose, never raise it. Stability across margins does not validate a clinical RP2D. The bootstrap band captures finite-cohort sampling uncertainty, not model-parameter or exposure-effect uncertainty; overlapping bands do not establish clinical equivalence.

7 Additional exploratory exercises

These optional extensions are outside the one-hour workshop. They expand Exercises 1-5 without adding another required exercise. Existing results means no new ODE solves; new simulations means rerunning a changed model or cohort; new evidence means data collection, fitting, or model qualification beyond this tutorial.

Suggested progression: choose one question, change one assumption at a time, and report what the comparison can and cannot establish. Preserve patient identities across paired comparisons and record seeds and settings. Source any new numerical settings, or explicitly label them as teaching sensitivity assumptions rather than estimated biological effects.

7.1 Extend Exercise 1: QSP mechanisms and treatment response

  1. Compare another treatment (existing results). Extend selected_arms to include Lebrikizumab or another already-simulated arm. Compare drug_params and EASI trajectories with Dupilumab and Placebo. Deliver a plot and a biological explanation; this is not a clinical head-to-head comparison.
  2. Trace mechanism to outcome (existing results). Follow an inhibited cytokine through the equations to skin-barrier and pathogen states and then EASI. Deliver a mechanism diagram and an early-versus-late response comparison explaining why target inhibition and clinical improvement need not share a timescale.
  3. Challenge the baseline (new simulations). Compare the shared typical-patient baseline with individual equilibration using each patient’s QSP parameters. Verify convergence and calculate improvement from each patient’s own pretreatment EASI. Deliver baseline-severity and responder-rate comparisons; report equilibration failures rather than silently discarding them.

7.2 Extend Exercise 2: PopPK regimens and model structure

  1. Separate loading and maintenance (existing results, then new simulations). Compare the supplied schedules, then alter loading, maintenance, or interval one at a time. Deliver concentration profiles and trough comparisons separating early from sustained exposure. Keep concentration units and the day-based PK clock explicit; equal total administered dose need not imply equal profiles.
  2. Test a simpler model (new simulations). Compare the supplied two-compartment, linear-plus-saturable model with a deliberately reduced alternative. Examine post-loading distribution, washout, troughs, and concentrations around km. Deliver prediction differences and acceptance criteria; removing distribution or saturable clearance may lose behavior relevant to dose selection.
  3. Distinguish covariates from random effects (new simulations). Change a supported covariate such as body weight while holding ETAs and regimen fixed, then vary PK ETAs with covariates fixed. Deliver paired concentration plots separating these contributions. Use a justified covariate range rather than extrapolating without evidence.

7.3 Extend Exercise 3: Sampling distributions and cohort size

  1. Compare log and natural scales (no new ODE solves). Tabulate means, variances, medians, and tail quantiles for normal and variance-matched uniform ETA draws and individual k1. Explain why equal log-scale variance and the same exp(lk1) need not preserve natural-scale means or tails.
  2. Check sampling stability (no new ODE solves). Repeat draws across recorded seeds and increasing n_demo. Deliver convergence plots for sample moments or quantiles, distinguishing finite-sample fluctuations from distributional differences. A single seed cannot establish which family fits real patients better.
  3. Propagate the alternative distribution (new simulations). Explicitly supply alternative ETAs through the event-table approach used by vpop_roster; changing the histogram chunk alone does not change solver sampling. Keep other draws paired and compare EASI trajectories and EASI-75. Deliver a sensitivity comparison, not a claim of population recalibration.

7.4 Extend Exercise 4: Correlation within and between models

  1. Check covariance validity (no new ODE solves). Sweep explicitly labelled illustrative rho settings in Sigma_th2. Check symmetry, unchanged marginal variances, and positive definiteness before sampling. Deliver eigenvalue checks and explain why arbitrary pairwise correlations can produce an invalid joint distribution.
  2. Compare correlations across scales (no new ODE solves, then optional new simulations). Inspect all three Th2 cytokine-production pairs on ETA and exponentiated parameter scales. Deliver correlation tables and scatterplots; equal marginal spreads do not establish independence. Optionally propagate valid blocks into paired QSP cohorts to compare response consequences.
  3. Design a cross-model covariance study (new evidence). Specify paired individual PK, disease-biomarker, and longitudinal response measurements that could identify covariance between PK and QSP ETAs. Deliver a data and identifiability plan before extending the joint covariance matrix. Separate cohorts or a shared seed cannot estimate this relationship.

7.5 Extend Exercise 5: Integrated mechanisms and dose selection

  1. Inspect the full integration chain (existing results, then new simulations). Align concentration, Emax-derived inhibition, and EASI trajectories for the same virtual patients and compare with fixed inhibition. Deliver plots locating where the mechanisms diverge. Extend to another dose or interval, preserving roster identities and the PK-days/QSP-weeks conversion.
  2. Refine the grid and decision rule (existing results, then new simulations). Start with the 0/5/10-percentage-point margins, then add a justified intermediate dose near the selection boundary. Deliver a table showing dependence on dose grid, margin, and assessment time. Keep loading and interval conventions explicit; classroom margins are not clinical thresholds.
  3. Bootstrap the decision (existing results). Resample the same patient IDs jointly across all doses, calculate paired response differences, and reapply the dose-selection rule. Deliver selection frequencies for each tested dose. These quantify finite-cohort stability conditional on the model, not the probability of a true clinical RP2D; overlapping pointwise bands do not establish equivalence.
  4. Separate PK and disease variability (new simulations). Compare PK-only, QSP-only, and joint-variability scenarios with matched underlying draws and explicit typical values for the fixed block. Deliver exposure and response summaries. Do not assume the contributions add linearly in a nonlinear model.
  5. Challenge the exposure-effect link (new simulations, then new evidence). Run labelled Emax and EC50 sensitivity scenarios and tabulate changes in curve shape and selected dose. Propose fitting the link to paired concentration and target-engagement observations across doses and time, adding delay or a Hill slope only if supported. Deliver a sensitivity table and held-out validation plan; scenarios are not full parameter-uncertainty propagation.
  6. Plan qualified dose selection and a virtual trial (new evidence, then new simulations). Define population, endpoint/time, feasible regimens, clinically justified benefit criteria, and safety constraints. Identify calibration and held-out validation gaps, including placebo and the exposure-effect link. Deliver an evidence-gap table and a repeated-trial simulation plan using justified sample sizes and assumptions. Separate cohort, parameter, and structural uncertainty; without safety evidence and qualification, retain only an illustrative efficacy candidate.
  7. Scale the computation (new simulations). Profile a small linked run; test caching dose-independent setup, coarse-to-refined grids, or parallel patient-dose solves. Deliver runtime and agreement checks against the original solver. A surrogate requires held-out full-solve validation. Parallelism reduces wall time, not solve count; cost is not inherently quadratic in dose count alone.

8 Appendix: assumptions and limitations

This appendix collects source-provenance and modelling assumptions that are useful for interpreting the tutorial results.

8.1 QSP model elements and sources

View structural elements and sources
Element Source
14 ODEs (skin barrier, pathogens, Th1-Th22, 7 cytokines, OX40L) Paper Sec 2.2 (14 ODEs, 51 parameters); reference implementation AD_QSP_model.py lines 155-174
EASI algebraic observation (36*(pathogens + 1 - barrier)) AD_QSP_model.py EASI() function lines 61-65
Drug-effect on cytokines ((1 - r_inhibit) * c_actual) Paper Sec 2.3 (r_inhibit = 0.99 for antibodies)
Tralokinumab e_a2 = 0.4396 multiplier Paper Sec 4.2 (Discussion, “e_a2 = 0.44”); AD_QSP_model.py line 140
rIFNg additive skin concentration (c_rifng = 210) Paper Sec 2.3 (Eq. for c_IFNg); AD_QSP_model.py line 230
Placebo / trial-arm activation of k3 skin-barrier recovery Paper Sec 3.3 (“k3 corresponds to placebo effects”); AD_QSP_model.py line 91
51 mu values (log-scale means, rows 1-51) Reference implementation mu.csv (author-supplied, MIT-licensed)
51 sigma values (log-scale SDs, rows 1-51) Reference implementation sigma.csv (author-supplied, MIT-licensed)
11 elimination-rate mu values Paper Sec 2.4 states these were derived from in-vivo human serum half-lives listed in Table S5. Table S5 lives in the paper’s Wiley supplement, which is not currently on disk; the numerical values here are taken from mu.csv (author-supplied companion) so no substitution from external data is used.
Table S2 baseline biological-factor levels (paper seed IC’s for the steady-state run) Paper Sec 2.4 references Table S2; the numerical seed values (0.5931, 0.4069, 3.1, …) are reproduced from AD_QSP_model.py lines 183-198.
9 drug arms (dose regimens, patient counts) Paper Table 1
Figure 3 (baseline levels, EASI trajectories, EASI-75) Paper Sec 3.2, Figure 3
Full assumptions and deviations
  • Paper supplement (SI Section 3 with the S1 Table of ODEs, Table S3 with r_inhibit derivations, Tables S4/S5 with the 51 mu and sigma parameter values) is not currently on disk. The parameter values (mu.csv, sigma.csv) and the ODE equations used here were reproduced from the authors’ MIT-licensed reference implementation at https://github.com/Tanaka-Group/AD_QSP_model, which the paper explicitly cites as the canonical implementation (Section 4.6: “The code of the QSP model is available at …”). The failed auto-acquisition of the Wiley supplement is recorded in needs_acquisition.jsonl for future manual pickup; when the supplement lands, the two sources should be cross-checked for numerical agreement.
  • Table S3 r_inhibit derivations from IC50 and skin drug concentrations are not on disk. The r_inhibit = 0.99 for antibodies and r_inhibit = 0.44 for tralokinumab (via e_a2 = 0.4396) are used as stated in the paper’s Section 2.3 and Section 4.2 respectively; the derivations of these two values from IC50 + skin concentration data (paper Section 3.4 and Table S3) cannot be independently verified from the on-disk sources.
  • Table S5 elimination-rate half-lives are not on disk. The paper states these were derived from published in-vivo human serum half-lives. The numerical mu values used for ld1, ld8, ld9, ld10-d17 come from mu.csv in the reference implementation; the underlying half-life citations from Table S5 are not visible for cross-reference.
  • Vignette skips PKNCA. The paper’s efficacy endpoint (EASI-75 at 24 weeks) is not an NCA quantity; there is no dose-and-eliminate PK profile to integrate. Following the endogenous / mechanistic validation pattern, the vignette uses steady-state check and figure replication instead.
  • Between-patient variability interpretation. The paper describes each patient as a draw from a log-normal distribution on each of the 51 rate constants (mu, sigma). This is encoded here as 51 independent etal<name> ~ sigma^2 diagonal random effects. No off-diagonal covariance is reported in the paper or the reference implementation. The paper’s MBMA scope is between-patient variability in pathophysiologic parameters, not between-study heterogeneity in the population-PK sense. “Correlated PopSP sampling” builds one illustrative, biologically-motivated exception to this diagonal-OMEGA assumption (a Th2-pathway cytokine-production block) purely to demonstrate the technique and its downstream effect; the correlation itself is not estimated from data and is not used anywhere else in this document except where explicitly built into vpop_roster.
  • Drug-effect parameters exposed as ini() overrides. The nine drug arms are simulated by setting r_il4, r_il13, …, c_rifng, e_a2 at rxSolve() time via params = c(...). Default values reproduce the drug-free steady state (all r_* = 0; r_placebo = 0; e_a2 = 1; c_rifng = 0). Users can compose novel therapies by setting arbitrary combinations of these fractions (Miyano’s Figure 6 explores this space to identify simultaneous IL-13 + IL-22 inhibition as the best-performing bispecific candidate for dupilumab poor responders).
  • Vignette cohort size. The vignette uses n = 50 per arm to stay inside the pkgdown render time budget. The paper’s Figure 3 uses 1000 virtual patients per arm and 1000 repeated simulated trials for 95% CIs. The qualitative shape (drug ordering, response-rate direction) reproduces at n = 50; the exact numerical Figure-3 CIs do not.
  • PK-specific assumptions (the combined literature-based variability components, the illustrative Emax link, and PK-QSP ETA independence) are listed beside the PK walkthrough. Concentration is in mg/L; the linked simulations explicitly convert PK days to QSP weeks.
